planting.note: Plant in spring in a raised, gravel-mulched bed with sharp drainage so winter moisture never pools around the crown.

directions: Pediocactus simpsonii, the mountain ball cactus, grows wild from the high plains of South Dakota and Wyoming south through the Rocky Mountains to Arizona and New Mexico, often above 7,000 feet in elevation, higher than almost any other North American cactus. Winter-hardy stock from northern populations is documented surviving temperatures near -20 degrees F, making it one of the most cold-tolerant cacti in cultivation, though it demands gritty, fast-draining mineral soil and bone-dry winter dormancy to avoid crown rot. In April and May it produces a ring of pink to cream flowers around the crown of its low, solitary or slowly clustering globose stem. Best sited in a raised bed, scree, or trough where winter moisture drains away instantly from the root crown.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Site on a south- or west-facing slope or raised gravel berm so winter precipitation drains away from the crown.

directions: Echinocereus coccineus is native to the mountains and high desert of New Mexico, Arizona, and southern Colorado, where it forms low, sprawling mounds of many cylindrical stems in rocky, well-drained soils. Long treated as a variety of the closely related claret cup cactus (Echinocereus triglochidiatus), it is now recognized by Flora of North America as a distinct tetraploid species, separable in the field mainly by range and by slightly greener stigmas and denser spination. Northern-provenance plants are documented hardy to roughly -20 degrees F in Zone 5 gardens when grown in raised, gritty berms that shed winter moisture, and in late spring the mounds erupt in a ring of brilliant scarlet-orange, cup-shaped flowers that hummingbirds favor. Excellent winter drainage is essential, since cold alone rarely kills it but cold combined with wet soil will.

planting.note: Set out nursery-propagated plants in spring in a trough or raised scree bed of mineral grit with no organic buildup around the crown.

directions: Escobaria sneedii is a diminutive, densely clustering pincushion cactus restricted in the wild to limestone outcrops of the Franklin Mountains along the Texas-New Mexico border, a region with cold, dry winters and intense summer sun. Specialty cold-hardy cactus growers report it thriving from USDA Zone 4 into much warmer zones, and it has proven reliably winter-hardy in trough and rock gardens well outside its native range when given mineral, humus-free soil that drains instantly. Dense clumps of small white-spined cylindrical stems produce a flush of tiny pink to coral flowers each spring. Because wild populations are federally listed as threatened and very restricted in range, only nursery-propagated stock should ever be planted.
sources: New Mexico Rare Plants (University of New Mexico)
